timeline.title: Born in Florida, Missouri
timeline.text: Samuel Langhorne Clemens was born in the small town of Florida, Missouri. He was the sixth of seven children. He was born shortly after an appearance of Halley's Comet.

timeline.title: A river town childhood
timeline.text: When he was about four, the family moved to Hannibal, a port town on the Mississippi River. Hannibal later became the model for the town in Tom Sawyer and Huckleberry Finn.

timeline.title: His father dies
timeline.text: His father, John Marshall Clemens, died of pneumonia when Sam was 11. The family was left short of money.

timeline.title: Printer's apprentice
timeline.text: He left school after the fifth grade to become a printer's apprentice. Setting type by hand gave him a long, close education in words. By 1851 he was writing sketches for his brother Orion's newspaper.

timeline.place: New York, Philadelphia, St. Louis and Cincinnati, (United States)
timeline.title: A travelling printer
timeline.text: Around age 18 he left Hannibal and worked as a printer in several big cities.

timeline.title: Cub pilot on the Mississippi
timeline.text: The steamboat pilot Horace Bixby agreed to train him for 500 dollars, paid out of his first wages. Learning the whole river took more than two years before he earned his pilot's licence.

timeline.title: His brother Henry is lost
timeline.text: The steamboat Pennsylvania exploded. His younger brother Henry, who worked on the boat, died eight days later.

timeline.title: War ends the river years
timeline.text: The Civil War stopped most traffic on the Mississippi. He served about two weeks in a Confederate militia unit, the Marion Rangers, then left and followed Orion west to Nevada.

timeline.title: The name Mark Twain
timeline.text: Writing for the Territorial Enterprise newspaper, he first signed himself Mark Twain. On the river, 'mark twain' was the leadsman's call for two fathoms, or 12 feet, of safe water.

timeline.title: The Jumping Frog
timeline.text: His comic tale 'The Celebrated Jumping Frog of Calaveras County' appeared in the New York Saturday Press. It brought him national attention.

timeline.title: Letters from Hawaii
timeline.text: The Sacramento Union sent him to the Sandwich Islands, now Hawaii, as a reporter. His travel letters became the basis of his first public lectures.

timeline.place: Aboard the Quaker City, Mediterranean Sea
timeline.title: The Quaker City voyage
timeline.text: He sailed on the steamship Quaker City for a five-month trip to Europe and the Holy Land, writing travel letters as he went.

timeline.title: The Innocents Abroad
timeline.text: His letters from the voyage became The Innocents Abroad, a funny, sharp travel book and his first big success.

timeline.title: Marries Olivia Langdon
timeline.text: He married Olivia (Livy) Langdon in Elmira, New York. They would have four children.

timeline.title: First patent: a garment strap
timeline.text: He received US patent 121,992 for an adjustable, detachable strap for garments, meant to replace suspenders. It was the first of his three patents.

timeline.title: Roughing It, and a loss
timeline.text: Roughing It, his book about the West, was published. The same year, while the family lived in Buffalo, their son Langdon died of diphtheria at 19 months.

timeline.title: The self-pasting scrapbook
timeline.text: He patented a scrapbook with gum already on the pages, so users only had to wet them (US 140,245). It sold more than 25,000 copies.

timeline.title: The Hartford house
timeline.text: The family moved into a 25-room house on Farmington Avenue. They lived there for 17 years, and he wrote many of his best-known books there. The house is now a museum.

timeline.title: Tom Sawyer
timeline.text: The Adventures of Tom Sawyer was published, drawing on his boyhood in Hannibal.

timeline.title: Life on the Mississippi
timeline.text: He published Life on the Mississippi, part memoir of his piloting years and part account of a return trip down the river.

timeline.title: Huckleberry Finn
timeline.text: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn was published first in Britain and Canada, then in the United States on 18 February 1885. A library in Concord, Massachusetts, banned it in 1885 as 'trash'. Ernest Hemingway later said modern American literature comes from it. Its frequent use of a racial slur keeps it debated in schools today.

timeline.title: A history game, and a publishing house
timeline.text: He received his third patent, for a history trivia game (US 324,535). His own publishing firm, Charles L. Webster and Company, run with his nephew by marriage, had early success with the memoirs of Ulysses S. Grant.

timeline.title: Leaving Hartford
timeline.text: Short of money after bad investments, the family closed the Hartford house and moved to Europe, where living was cheaper.

timeline.title: Bankrupt
timeline.text: His publishing firm failed, and he had sunk about 300,000 dollars between 1880 and 1894 into the Paige typesetting machine, which broke down often and was beaten by the Linotype. Advised by his friend Henry H. Rogers, he filed for bankruptcy and moved his copyrights to his wife, Livy, to protect them from creditors.

timeline.place: Around the world (Australia, India and other parts of the British Empire)
timeline.title: The world lecture tour
timeline.text: Though the law no longer required it, he set out on a year-long lecture tour to pay his creditors in full. He was about 100,000 dollars in debt. He spoke to crowds across the British Empire, including Australia and India.

timeline.title: Susy dies
timeline.text: While he was still abroad, his daughter Susy died of meningitis at 24, while visiting the Hartford house. The family never lived there again.

timeline.title: Following the Equator
timeline.text: His account of the tour, Following the Equator, was published by the American Publishing Company of Hartford. The family lived mainly in England and Austria from 1897 to 1899.

timeline.title: Home with debts paid
timeline.text: He returned to the United States, having earned enough to pay off his debts. Henry Rogers had managed his money until every creditor was paid.

timeline.title: Livy dies
timeline.text: His wife Olivia died at the Villa di Quarto near Florence.

timeline.title: Honoured at Oxford
timeline.text: Oxford University gave him an honorary Doctor of Letters. Yale (1901) and the University of Missouri (1902) had already honoured him.

timeline.title: Jean dies
timeline.text: His youngest daughter Jean died on Christmas Eve at Stormfield, his house in Redding. That year he had said he expected to 'go out' with Halley's Comet.

timeline.title: Death at Stormfield
timeline.text: He died of a heart attack at Stormfield, one day after Halley's Comet came closest to the Sun. He was buried in the Langdon family plot at Woodlawn Cemetery in Elmira, New York.

timeline.title: The Mark Twain Prize
timeline.text: The Kennedy Center first awarded the Mark Twain Prize for American Humor, to Richard Pryor. It is given every year in his name.

timeline.title: The autobiography, 100 years on
timeline.text: The first volume of his full autobiography was published, 100 years after his death, by the Mark Twain Project at the University of California.

patents.title: Improvement in Adjustable and Detachable Straps for Garments

patentsNote: Samuel L. Clemens held three US patents, each checked on Google Patents. Grant dates are from each record. For US 121,992 Google Patents shows no filing date (the specification is signed 9 September 1871), so it is null here. For US 140,245 the specification gives a filing date of 7 May 1873, while the Google Patents metadata field repeats the grant date; the specification date is used.

works.title: The Celebrated Jumping Frog of Calaveras County
works.text: A tall tale from the California mining camps that first made his name known across the country.

works.title: The Innocents Abroad
works.text: A comic travel book from his 1867 voyage to Europe and the Holy Land, poking fun at tourists, himself included.

works.title: Adjustable garment strap
works.text: An elastic strap to fasten garments, meant to replace suspenders (US 121,992).

works.title: Roughing It
works.text: His funny memoir of the Nevada and California years.

works.title: Self-pasting scrapbook
works.text: A scrapbook with gummed pages that only needed wetting (US 140,245). It sold more than 25,000 copies.

works.title: The Adventures of Tom Sawyer
works.text: A boy's adventures in a Mississippi river town based on Hannibal.

works.title: The Prince and the Pauper
works.text: A historical tale of two look-alike boys in Tudor England who swap places.

works.title: Life on the Mississippi
works.text: Memories of learning to pilot a steamboat, joined to a later trip down the river.

works.title: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn
works.text: Huck and Jim, who has escaped slavery, travel down the river on a raft. Praised and challenged ever since.

works.title: History trivia game
works.text: A board game for learning historical facts and dates (US 324,535).

works.title: A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court
works.text: A 19th-century American wakes up in King Arthur's England and tries to modernise it.

works.title: Pudd'nhead Wilson
works.text: A small-town story about two babies switched at birth, with each chapter opened by a short, wry saying from 'Pudd'nhead Wilson's Calendar'.

works.title: The world lecture tour
works.text: A year of talks across the British Empire, made to repay his creditors after the 1894 bankruptcy.

works.title: Following the Equator
works.text: His 712-page travel account of the lecture tour, mixing humour with sharp comments on empire.

works.title: King Leopold's Soliloquy
works.text: A satire attacking the brutal rule of King Leopold II of Belgium over the Congo.

works.title: Autobiography of Mark Twain, Volume 1
works.text: His autobiography in full, published a century after his death.
